lessons.title: The Atlas — every use of AI in public health and medicine
lessons.subtitle: The whole landscape on day one, so every later lesson has something to point at
lessons.description: The catalogue: ~95 applications across six problem shapes, with maturity labels and the cautionary canon. The course's front door, never finished.
lessons.practical: Add three rows to the Atlas from your own news feed this week. For each, answer the four questions. Note which question the source could not answer.

quiz.question: The atlas claims there are six shapes rather than hundreds of kinds of health AI. What does 'shape' refer to?
options: The data modality — tabular, image, text, or time series
The question being asked, which determines what evidence the claim owes you
The algorithm family being used, which determines the computational requirements and the training data volume
The clinical specialty in which the application is deployed
quiz.explanation: A shape is a property of the question, not of the method or the data. That is why the same gradient-boosted tree is shape 1 when it scores how surprising today's count is and shape 2 when it predicts next month's — and why each shape owes a different kind of evidence.

quiz.question: Match the shape to its classical ancestor: which pairing is correct?
options: Turn language into data — manual chart abstraction and coding
Detect the unusual — logistic regression and diagnostic tests
Choose an action — control charts and CUSUM applied to the decision variable
Find structure without labels — ARIMA and compartmental models
quiz.explanation: Shape 5's ancestor is manual chart abstraction. The others are misassigned: clustering's ancestor is cluster and factor analysis, anomaly detection's is control charts and CUSUM, and decision support's is operations research and decision analysis. Naming the ancestor is how you find the comparator a claim must beat.

quiz.question: The atlas names two cross-cutting layers alongside the six shapes. What does it claim about the first of them?
options: Evaluation and deployment are the same layer viewed at different scales
Almost every failure in the atlas is an evaluation failure, not a modelling failure
Evaluation matters most for regulator-cleared applications and least for early-stage research work
Evaluation is a reporting requirement that follows the modelling work
quiz.explanation: Evaluation decides whether a model is real, and deployment and governance decide whether a real model helps anyone. The stronger claim is the first: nearly everything in the cautionary canon failed on how it was evaluated rather than on how it was built.

quiz.question: A colleague brings you a new AI-in-health claim. What are the four questions the atlas puts it through?
options: Which shape · what comparator · how evaluated · maturity, honestly
Which population · what outcome · what comparator · what effect size
Which specialty · what regulator · what cost · what evidence grade
Which shape · what data · which model · what accuracy
quiz.explanation: Answer those four and the item becomes an atlas row; answer them in depth and it becomes a deep-dive page. Note the first one's escape hatch: if it does not fit any of the six shapes, that is itself a finding worth saying out loud.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the six cases in the atlas's cautionary canon?
options: Google Flu Trends — big data does not fix unstable predictors
AlphaFold — structural prediction outran its validation set
The AI Clinician — off-policy evaluation is not evidence
Obermeyer et al. 2019 — the label carries the bias
quiz.explanation: The canon is Google Flu Trends, the Epic Sepsis Model, Obermeyer et al., the Wynants COVID prognostic review, Beede et al. in Thailand, and the AI Clinician. Each teaches a distinct evaluation failure, which is why the atlas says the six read together teach more than a methods textbook.

quiz.question: The atlas keeps a visible list of what it is still missing. Why is that in the course rather than removed?
options: Regulatory guidance on medical education requires explicit disclosure of scope limitations in any training material
It is the course's to-do queue, and a living course states what it does not yet cover
To signal the course is provisional and should be treated with caution
Because the missing items are too technical for the intended audience
quiz.explanation: The course is marked `living`, and the gap list is where new entries come from. Stating what is not covered is also what stops a reader assuming the atlas is exhaustive — the same reason the genomic surveillance course carries an explicit `not_covered` block.

lessons.title: The six shapes
lessons.subtitle: A sorting reflex for the several claims a week you will read for the rest of your career
lessons.description: Classify any AI-in-health claim into one of six pattern-recognition problems in under a minute, and name the classical method it must beat.
topics: Reading a claim in four questions
lessons.practical: Build the claims register from the worked example, then add the three most recent AI-in-health items you have read. Filter for 'no comparator or internal-only evaluation' and see what it flags.

quiz.question: A gradient-boosted tree scores how surprising today's case count is. The same model, unchanged, is then used to predict next month's count. What happened to the shape?
options: It moved from shape 1 to shape 2
Nothing — the shape follows the algorithm
It became shape 3, because trees assign labels
Shapes do not apply to tree-based models
quiz.explanation: Shape is a property of the question, not the method. Scoring surprise is shape 1 (detect the unusual); predicting a future value is shape 2 (forecasting). The first option is the common error: people argue about algorithms because algorithms have names, but the question determines what evidence you need.

quiz.question: A paper proposes a new deep-learning method for tabular risk prediction and reports no comparison with logistic regression or gradient boosting. What is the best-supported inference?
options: The authors ran out of space
The comparison was probably unfavourable
Deep learning has no tabular comparator
Nothing can be inferred from an absence
quiz.explanation: Reporting a favourable comparison is essentially free, so its absence is selective rather than accidental. This is a base rate, not cynicism, and it is well supported here specifically: tabular deep learning reliably loses to gradient boosting on structured data.

quiz.question: Why is Google Flu Trends best described as a shape-straddling failure?
options: It relied on search data rather than clinical surveillance reports
It confused unsupervised clustering with supervised classification
It was evaluated as forecasting but sold as early warning
No classical comparator for influenza-like illness existed at the time
quiz.explanation: It was evaluated on whether it tracked ILI (shape 2) and marketed on whether it warned earlier (shape 1). Those require different evidence. A claim evaluated as one shape and sold as another is the most common failure mode in the field — and a sentinel ILI comparator did exist.

quiz.question: Which of these is the correct classical comparator for a claim in shape 5 (turn language into data)?
options: A seasonal naive forecast
Farrington/CUSUM on the same series
A pre-specified stratification
A human chart abstractor
quiz.explanation: Shape 5's ancestor is manual chart abstraction or coding. The others belong to shapes 2, 1 and 4 respectively. Note the wrinkle: the human comparator is itself imperfect, so agreement between abstractors must also be reported.

quiz.question: An anomaly detector, a forecaster and an image classifier walk into a review. Which owes you a proper scoring rule?
options: The forecaster only
All three
The classifier only
The anomaly detector only
quiz.explanation: Proper scoring rules (WIS, CRPS, log score) apply to probabilistic forecasts — shape 2. Shape 1 owes a false-alarm rate and timeliness at a matched threshold; shape 3 owes calibration and PPV at the deployment prevalence. Six shapes, six different debts.

quiz.question: A system flags unusual phrasing in outbreak reports to surface possible events. Which shape is it, and why is that not obvious?
options: Shape 5, because the input being processed is unstructured free text
Shape 1, because the question is whether this differs from expected
Shape 3, because each incoming report is assigned a label
Shape 4, because it groups similar reports without using labels
quiz.explanation: The question asked is 'is this different from what I expected?', which is shape 1 — the input modality does not set the shape. Text is merely a signal with no natural baseline, which is one of the three places machine learning genuinely adds something in this shape.

quiz.question: What does the second half of the course spine claim?
options: Larger models generalise better across settings and populations
Classical statistical methods win in essentially every application
What decides whether it works is the evaluation, not the model
Every shape eventually requires deep learning to reach usable accuracy
quiz.explanation: The spine has two halves: the field is six problems (which makes it learnable), and evaluation rather than modelling decides whether any of them works. The second half is why the course does not go out of date — methods churn, evaluation failures repeat.

lessons.title: Detect the unusual — anomaly detection and early warning
lessons.subtitle: The baseline is the science; the detector is the easy half
lessons.description: Shape 1. Why the baseline carries the science, Farrington/Noufaily as the benchmark, where ML genuinely adds, and evaluation at a matched false-alarm rate.
lessons.practical: Run the alpha sweep from the worked example on salmonella.agona. Choose the row a team that can investigate one signal per week should operate at, and state what timeliness you gave up.

quiz.question: An anomaly detector has two parts. Which carries the scientific content?
options: The threshold rule that converts a score into an alarm
The logic that routes an alarm to whoever investigates it
Both contribute roughly equally to detection performance
The model of 'expected'
quiz.explanation: The baseline model of what you expected is the entire scientific content; the threshold is a policy decision about tolerable false alarms. Most published effort goes into clever detectors, while most real-world failure comes from an inadequate baseline.

quiz.question: Weekly counts show variance far exceeding the mean. What breaks if you assume Poisson?
options: Thresholds become too tight and false alarms explode
Sensitivity falls to zero because the variance term dominates
Seasonality can no longer be represented in the baseline model
The linear trend term becomes unidentifiable and must be dropped
quiz.explanation: Overdispersion means the true spread is wider than Poisson allows, so a Poisson prediction interval is too narrow and the observed false-alarm rate far exceeds the nominal one. This is why Farrington uses a quasi-Poisson fit and why Noufaily improved the handling further.

quiz.question: Why must historical outbreaks be downweighted in the reference window?
options: They violate the independence assumption the GLM requires
They raise 'expected' and mask the current outbreak
They introduce spurious seasonality into the reference window
They shorten the effective baseline and widen the interval
quiz.explanation: If last year's epidemic sits in the baseline, expectation is inflated and this year's genuine excess falls below threshold. Every serious method in this family reweights or removes historical outliers for exactly this reason.

quiz.question: Mechanically, what is the Farrington/Noufaily algorithm?
options: A recurrent neural network trained on historical count data
A hidden Markov model alternating between outbreak and baseline states
A quasi-Poisson GLM with a one-sided prediction interval
A permutation test computed over matched seasonal windows
quiz.explanation: It fits an overdispersed Poisson GLM to counts from the same seasonal window in past years, with a trend and outlier reweighting, then alarms when the observation exceeds a one-sided upper prediction limit. Recognising it as a regression model with an interval is what stops each new detector looking like a new idea.

quiz.question: Where does machine learning most clearly beat the classical aberration stack?
options: A single weekly count series with five years of history
Series with strong seasonality
Low-count series near elimination
Many signals monitored simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Farrington is univariate, so 400 series means 400 multiple-comparison problems. Multivariate methods score a whole vector at once and can flag a pattern unremarkable in every individual series. On one well-behaved series with good history, the classical method is very hard to beat.

quiz.question: Two detectors are compared; the new one is earlier. What must be equalised first?
options: The false-alarm rate
Training-set size
The seasonal window
The outcome definition
quiz.explanation: Any detector looks earlier if allowed to alarm more often, so timeliness at unmatched false-alarm rates is meaningless. Fix the false-alarm rate — for example by tuning alpha — and only then compare timeliness.

quiz.question: A district's malaria counts trigger a highly significant alarm. What do you check first?
options: Whether the p-value survives correction for multiple comparisons
Whether the denominator or data pipeline changed
Whether the linear trend term was included in the baseline
Whether neighbouring districts alarmed in the same reporting week
quiz.explanation: The algorithm already established that the count exceeded expectation; it cannot say why. New clinics, changed case definitions, a lab switching assay, or a clerk clearing a backlog all produce significant, purely administrative anomalies — and in routine practice these outnumber real outbreaks.

quiz.question: Why is 'detected three weeks earlier' sometimes worth nothing?
options: Early signals are usually false once investigated properly
Because timeliness cannot be measured without a gold standard
Because response may still require laboratory confirmation
Because detecting earlier necessarily lowers specificity
quiz.explanation: Earlier is only better if something can be done earlier. This is the syndromic surveillance finding: it genuinely is earlier than lab confirmation and mostly did not change anyone's actions. Add alarm fatigue — once alarm PPV falls far enough, investigators stop investigating and system sensitivity goes to zero.

lessons.title: Predict what happens next — forecasting, and why the ensemble wins
lessons.subtitle: The shape where honesty is measurable, and is the thing being measured
lessons.description: Shape 2. Nowcasting vs forecasting vs early warning, reporting delay and the false decline, the classical toolkit as comparator, proper scoring rules, and the ensemble finding.
topics: Nowcasting vs forecasting vs early warning
lessons.practical: Plot the last twelve weeks of a surveillance series you work with as reported. Ask how much of the apparent decline is reporting delay. If you cannot answer, that is the finding.

quiz.question: An uncorrected real-time surveillance series appears to be declining. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Seasonal forcing is reducing transmission at this point in the year
The underlying epidemic has genuinely passed its peak
Case definitions were tightened during the reporting period
Reporting delay: the most recent points are incomplete counts
quiz.explanation: Cases are reported over days to weeks, so the last points of any real-time series are partial. An uncorrected series looks like it is falling at all times, including during exponential growth. Programmes have relaxed on this artefact more than once; nowcasting is the correction.

quiz.question: Two forecasters report an identical median of 100. One states a 95% interval of [98,102], the other [60,140]. What does MAE tell you?
options: Nothing — MAE depends only on the median, which is identical
That the narrow forecaster is better calibrated than the wide one
That the wide forecaster has higher uncertainty and worse accuracy
That neither forecast can be scored without the full distribution
quiz.explanation: MAE is a point-forecast metric and cannot distinguish them, ever. One claims to know the answer to plus or minus 2 and the other to plus or minus 40, and the metric is blind to the difference. That blindness is precisely the incentive to be over-confident.

quiz.question: Using the interval score, at what truth value does the narrow interval [98,102] become worse than the wide [60,140]?
options: Only once the truth exceeds 140, outside both intervals
At 104 — just 2 beyond the stated interval
Not until roughly 180, where both are heavily penalised
At 110, once the median error exceeds ten percent
quiz.explanation: Computed: the narrow interval scores 4.0 when the truth is 100 and 44.0 at 103, crossing the wide interval's constant 80.0 at 104. A proper score rewards sharpness when it is justified and punishes it sharply when it is not — which is exactly the behaviour you want.

quiz.question: What is the central empirical finding of organised infectious-disease forecasting?
options: Mechanistic transmission models consistently outperform statistical ones
Machine-learning methods dominate once enough covariates are included
A simple combination of many models beats almost every individual model
Forecast accuracy has improved steadily with increasing model complexity
quiz.explanation: Across FluSight, the US COVID-19 Forecast Hub and the European hub, the ensemble — often just the median of submissions — outperformed nearly every individual model and was far more reliable over time. Two mechanisms: error cancellation across independent models, and robustness to regime change.

quiz.question: Why can only a mechanistic model answer 'what if we close schools?'
options: Mechanistic models are fitted to longer historical time series
Statistical models cannot produce probabilistic outputs at all
Mechanistic models have lower forecast error at long horizons
Because the intervention is not in a statistical model's feature space
quiz.explanation: Counterfactuals require parameters that mean something — contact rates, transmission probabilities. A time-series model can say what will happen but not what would happen if, because school closure is not a variable it contains. Statistical for prediction, mechanistic for counterfactuals.

quiz.question: Why are tree-based methods structurally unsuited to forecasting an epidemic peak?
options: They cannot predict a value larger than any they have observed
They require far more training data than surveillance provides
They cannot incorporate seasonal or cyclical covariates
They produce point estimates without any uncertainty interval
quiz.explanation: A tree predicts by averaging observed outcomes in a leaf, so its output is bounded by the training range. That is what a tree is, not a tuning problem — and it is fatal when the quantity of interest is a peak higher than anything yet seen.

quiz.question: A colleague reports an excellent RMSE for their district-level forecast. What should you ask for first?
options: The number of covariates included in the model
The skill relative to a seasonal-naive baseline
The software package and version they used
The computational cost of refitting the model weekly
quiz.explanation: A raw error figure is uninterpretable: an MAE of 12 means nothing until you know the naive forecast scores 15. Report skill relative to the boring baseline, and frequently it turns out to be negative. After that, ask for intervals and coverage.

quiz.question: An ensemble is built from twenty variants of the same SEIR model. Why is this not an ensemble in the useful sense?
options: Twenty members is too few for error cancellation to operate
Mechanistic models cannot be combined by taking a median
They share assumptions, so the combination inherits them
Compartmental models are not scored by proper rules
quiz.explanation: Diversity does the work. Error cancellation requires members that err in different directions, and robustness to regime change requires members that fail under different conditions. Twenty variants of one model fail together, so the ensemble inherits the shared assumption rather than averaging it away.

lessons.title: Labels from databases — tabular pattern recognition and the record of the decision
lessons.subtitle: The row does not describe a patient; it describes what was done to a patient
lessons.description: Shape 3 from tables. Found data and its fingerprints, missingness as a clinical decision, the tabular leakage catalogue, the label as a measurement, and what a risk model owes you before it triggers anything.
lessons.practical: Take a risk score used where you work. List its features and mark each twice: available at prediction time or determined afterwards, and measurement of biology or trace of a decision.

quiz.question: In the worked example, 'was a test ordered?' reached AUC 0.87 while the test's value reached 0.61. What has the model learned?
options: A genuine physiological signal that the test value measures imprecisely
An artefact of the simulation that would not occur in real records
The effect of the test itself on the patient's subsequent outcome
The clinician's suspicion, because ordering a test is a judgement
quiz.explanation: A troponin is measured because someone suspected a cardiac event. The missingness indicator therefore encodes clinical judgement, which predicts outcome well. It is the tabular analogue of confounded acquisition in imaging: the presence of a value records the encounter, just as an image records the encounter.

quiz.question: A hospital changes policy so that every admission gets the test. What happens to a model that leaned on the indicator?
options: The indicator becomes constant and carries no information at all
It recalibrates automatically as the new data accumulate
Its discrimination improves because missing data are eliminated
It continues to perform as before, since the values are unchanged
quiz.explanation: Nothing about the patients changed. A memo changed. The feature that carried most of the model's performance becomes uninformative, and the failure is silent — which is why the question to ask of any feature is whether it will still exist and still mean the same thing where the model runs.

quiz.question: Why is standard advice to 'impute the missing values' hazardous in health records?
options: Imputation methods assume normality that laboratory values rarely satisfy
Missingness is often signal, and signal contingent on a testing policy
Imputation is computationally prohibitive at electronic-record scale
Imputed values cannot be used in tree-based models without adjustment
quiz.explanation: Imputation treats missingness as a nuisance to repair. In health data it frequently carries the clinician's judgement — and that signal is valid today and gone tomorrow if testing policy changes. Neither imputing nor keeping the indicator is automatically right; making the choice silently is what is wrong.

quiz.question: Which observational-study bias does the 'patients who completed treatment' feature correspond to?
options: Confounding by indication from the prescriber's choice
Differential misclassification of the treatment exposure
Immortal time bias, since the group requires survival to be defined
Regression dilution caused by measurement error in the exposure
quiz.explanation: Completing treatment requires surviving it, so the group cannot include those who died during it. It is a classic pharmaco-epidemiological trap and it walks straight into feature engineering — which is why every tabular leakage pattern has an observational-study name you already know.

quiz.question: What does a SHAP plot establish about a model?
options: That its predictions are calibrated across the risk range
That its features were all available at prediction time
That its performance will transfer to an external site
What the model used, but not whether the model is right
quiz.explanation: Explainability is not validation. A confounded model produces a beautifully interpretable explanation of its confound — the SHAP plot would have shown 'test ordered' as the top feature and looked entirely sensible. Interpretability tells you what happened inside; it says nothing about external validity.

quiz.question: What is the documented finding about deep learning on tabular data?
options: Gradient boosting reliably outperforms it across typical benchmarks
It surpasses gradient boosting once feature counts exceed a threshold
The two are equivalent given sufficient hyperparameter tuning
It performs better on imbalanced outcomes but worse on balanced ones
quiz.explanation: The finding is consistent rather than occasional, so when a neural network is proposed for a spreadsheet the burden of proof lies with the proposer. 'We used deep learning' describes effort, not quality.

quiz.question: Why does resampling to fix class imbalance require an extra step?
options: It reduces the effective sample size and widens confidence intervals
It distorts calibration, which is the property a threshold decision needs
It introduces duplicate patients across the train and test partitions
It prevents tree-based methods from splitting on rare categories
quiz.explanation: Over-sampling, SMOTE and class weights change the apparent outcome prevalence, so predicted probabilities no longer mean what they say. If you resample, recalibrate afterwards and report that you did. And remember accuracy is meaningless on a rare outcome: predicting 'no' for everyone scores 97% at 3% prevalence.

quiz.question: What does 'case' mean in a surveillance database, and why does it matter for a model?
options: A laboratory-confirmed infection meeting the standard case definition
An episode of care coded for reimbursement by the treating facility
Detected and reported, so the model learns the geography of surveillance
An incident infection dated by symptom onset rather than by report
quiz.explanation: A proxy inherits the artefacts and inequities of the process that produced it. Any model trained on reported cases learns where surveillance reaches as much as where disease is — the working epidemiologist's version of the cost-for-need substitution in the Obermeyer case.

lessons.title: Labels from pixels — images, video, and what the model is really looking at
lessons.subtitle: You cannot audit the input, so you must audit the acquisition
lessons.description: Shape 3 from pixels. What a convolutional network computes, confounded acquisition as the signature failure, who is in the training data, what predicts generalisation, and what video's extra dimension buys.
lessons.practical: Run the worked example, then weaken the confound until the genuine signal dominates. Note the association strength at which it flips — that is how strong a confound must be to matter.

quiz.question: Why is confounded acquisition described as a validity problem rather than overfitting?
options: Because the model has far too many free parameters for the available sample size
Because the validation split was drawn before the preprocessing steps were applied
Because the labels were assigned inconsistently by several different clinicians
Because the confounded signal is real and reproduces in every fold of the archive
quiz.explanation: The signal genuinely exists and is stable within the dataset, so cross-validation confirms rather than exposes it. What fails is the mapping to deployment, where the confound no longer accompanies the disease. Overfitting is a variance problem; this is a validity problem, and internal validation cannot detect it.

quiz.question: What is the shared mechanism behind surgical skin markings, rulers, portable X-rays and chest drains?
options: All four are present because someone had already formed a diagnostic suspicion
All four degrade the effective image resolution in ways the network exploits
All four are introduced by lossy digital compression during image storage
All four occur disproportionately on older and poorly calibrated equipment
quiz.explanation: A medical image records a clinical encounter, not just a patient, and the encounter carries information about the diagnosis. The clinician marked the lesion they meant to excise, placed the scale beside the worrying one, sent the portable machine to the sicker patient, and inserted the drain after diagnosing the pneumothorax.

quiz.question: In the dermatology case, what makes the skin-tone problem worse than simply 'performs less well on darker skin'?
options: Images of darker skin compress differently and lose diagnostic detail
Skin type was frequently not recorded in evaluation sets, so the gap was unmeasurable
The conditions themselves present identically across every skin phototype
Only dermoscopy images were affected, while clinical photographs were fine
quiz.explanation: A known limitation can be designed around — a different threshold, different referral, a warning to the user. An unmeasured one is simply distributed as harm. Purpose-built diverse test sets had to be constructed before the gap could even be stated, and when it could, performance dropped.

quiz.question: Which single feature best predicts that an imaging model will survive deployment?
options: A larger and more recent network architecture than the published baseline
A higher area under the curve on the original development dataset
A label drawn from a reference independent of the clinician being replaced
A substantially greater total number of training images than competitors
quiz.explanation: A bacteriological or histopathological reference standard makes a far stronger claim than agreement with the person the model would replace. Architecture and dataset size are rarely the story in this shape; the data, the label and the acquisition are. Development AUC says nothing about transfer.

quiz.question: Why must video datasets be split at patient level rather than frame level?
options: Frame-level splits produce class imbalance that cannot be corrected
Video frames cannot be shuffled without corrupting the codec
Patient-level splits are required by data protection law, not statistics
Frames within a video are highly correlated, so random splits put near-identical images on both sides
quiz.explanation: The same patient and nearly the same image end up in train and test, which is leakage and produces spectacular, entirely fake performance. This is the temporal-correlation form of the same leakage problem covered in lesson 9.

quiz.question: AI-guided obstetric ultrasound lets an untrained operator obtain a reliable gestational-age estimate. Why is this the strongest design pattern in imaging AI?
options: It moves a skill down the cadre ladder rather than replacing a specialist's judgement
It reaches higher accuracy than trained sonographers
It removes the need for any imaging equipment
It works without any reference standard for validation
quiz.explanation: In a system with no sonographers the counterfactual is not a worse estimate, it is no estimate. Framing AI as replacing a missing specialist gives a measurable health-systems benefit, whereas matching a present specialist is a benchmark contest — the same distinction that separated TB CAD from dermatology AI.

quiz.question: A radiologist is shown only the non-anatomical parts of a set of images and can guess the diagnosis fairly well. What have you learned?
options: The images are of insufficient diagnostic quality
There is a confound the model will preferentially learn
The radiologist is unusually skilled at pattern recognition
The label noise in the dataset is too high to model
quiz.explanation: That is the practical test for confounded acquisition. If non-anatomical content predicts the label, the model will use it, because it is easier to learn than the pathology — and internal validation will reward it for doing so.

lessons.title: Finding structure — clustering, embeddings, and clusters that are not there
lessons.subtitle: The only shape where the model defines the answer, so it cannot be contradicted by its own output
lessons.description: Shape 4. Why standard diagnostics report structure in pure noise, replication as the only honest validation, what a UMAP does not license you to conclude, and the ethics of clustering people.
lessons.practical: Take any clustering you have done or read about and compute the permutation null: run the identical pipeline on data with the structure destroyed, and report the observed value beside the null distribution.

quiz.question: 300 points drawn uniformly at random gave mean silhouette values of 0.36 to 0.41 across k=2 to 6. What does that establish?
options: That the silhouette is an unreliable statistic and should not be used
That uniform random data contains weak but genuine latent structure
That internal metrics are interpretable only against a null comparison
That k-means is the wrong algorithm for low-dimensional data
quiz.explanation: A silhouette near 0.4 reads as moderate real structure in isolation, and here it came from noise. Genuinely separated Gaussians reached 0.86. So 0.39 versus 0.86 is informative while 0.39 alone is not — which makes running your pipeline on a null and reporting both the cheap fix nobody applies.

quiz.question: Why can a within-cluster sum of squares plot mislead on pure noise?
options: It cannot be computed when clusters have unequal sizes
It is undefined for k greater than the intrinsic dimensionality
It requires the number of clusters to be specified in advance
It falls smoothly, so an elbow can be read where none exists
quiz.explanation: On the noise example WSS fell 30 to 18 to 12 to 10 to 8 — a smooth decline that an elbow reading interprets as k=3 or 4. The clusters were also balanced and plausible-looking, which is exactly how a real finding presents. The gap statistic formalises the null comparison the elbow lacks.

quiz.question: What does the spatial scan statistic do that most clustering methods omit?
options: It compares the most extreme window against its null distribution
It constrains cluster shapes to administrative boundaries
It requires no assumptions about the underlying population at risk
It identifies the optimal number of clusters automatically
quiz.explanation: It asks whether the most extreme cluster is more extreme than chance would produce given that thousands of windows were examined, using a Monte Carlo null. That is shape 4 with the multiple-comparisons problem taken seriously, and it is the comparator any machine-learning clustering claim on spatial data should face.

quiz.question: With no labels, what is the strongest available validation of a discovered structure?
options: A high silhouette coefficient on the derivation dataset
Replication of the same groups in an independent dataset
Stability of the solution across random initialisations
Agreement between two different clustering algorithms
quiz.explanation: Replication in a different cohort, country or year is the strongest evidence and the one most often skipped. Also useful: a null comparison, external validity of the groups on something you did not cluster on, and stability under perturbation. Internal metrics cannot establish reality.

quiz.question: In a UMAP plot, which feature is approximately trustworthy?
options: The distances between separate clusters
The relative sizes of the visible clusters
Local neighbourhood structure around each point
The number of distinct blobs that appear
quiz.explanation: Only local neighbourhoods are approximately preserved. Between-cluster distances and cluster sizes are not meaningful — the algorithm deliberately expands sparse regions and compresses dense ones — and the number of visible blobs depends on hyperparameters and can be tuned into or out of existence. Use it to look, never to conclude.

quiz.question: Why does an embedding's notion of 'similar' require scrutiny?
options: Embeddings are stochastic, so repeated runs disagree
High-dimensional distances are undefined without normalisation
Embeddings cannot represent categorical clinical variables
It is inherited from whatever data the embedding was trained on
quiz.explanation: A clinical-note embedding trained on US discharge summaries encodes US documentation habits as similarity. So the geometry you go on to cluster is not a neutral space but a model of someone else's data — and the clusters you find are partly a property of that inheritance.

quiz.question: What is the distinctive ethical question when the objects being clustered are people?
options: What happens to someone because of their assigned group, and can they contest it
Whether the clustering algorithm satisfies a formal fairness criterion
Whether consent was obtained for the specific clustering method used
Whether the cluster labels are anonymised before publication
quiz.explanation: A discovered subgroup becomes an administrative category, then a resource-allocation category, and eventually a fact about people rather than a feature of a dataset. HIV molecular clustering is the live case: it identifies people whose viruses are related, which is an inference about transmission that they did not consent to.

lessons.title: Language into data — clinical NLP, LLMs, and AI in the consultation
lessons.subtitle: The shape where the hard part is the label, not the model
lessons.description: Shape 5. Negation and hedging as case-definition problems, the pre-LLM stack and why it survives, RAG scored twice, and what the AMIE and ambient-scribe evidence actually shows.
lessons.practical: Write the case definition you would hand an annotator for a confirmed case in your own disease area, then list the sentences that stay ambiguous under it. If none are ambiguous, the definition is too vague.

quiz.question: Of the six failure modes in clinical text extraction, how many are really case-definition problems?
options: All six
Four
Two
None — they are all parsing problems
quiz.explanation: Negation, hedging, temporality and experiencer are all decisions about what counts as a case, not engineering problems. Abbreviation collision and multilingual text are genuine NLP problems. Recognising the split is the epidemiologist's main contribution to a language project.

quiz.question: 'No improvement on TB therapy after 8 weeks.' A negation-aware extractor marks this as not a TB case. Why is it wrong?
options: 'No' does not function as a negation trigger in clinical text
Eight weeks falls outside the algorithm's negation scope window
The trigger negates the improvement, not the diagnosis
'TB therapy' is a treatment mention rather than a diagnosis mention
quiz.explanation: The negation has scope, and here it falls on 'improvement' — the patient plainly has tuberculosis. No amount of trigger-list tuning fixes this; it requires scope, and scope requires the case definition to state what is being negated.

quiz.question: Why might a rule-based extractor be preferred over an LLM for a statutory notification pipeline?
options: It is more accurate on every task
It handles multilingual notes better
It needs no case definition
It is auditable and produces stable output
quiz.explanation: You can point at the line that produced a decision, and it returns the same output next month. Neither holds for a generative model. For anything feeding official statistics, auditability and stability can outweigh a few points of F1.

quiz.question: A RAG system answers a question incorrectly. What must be checked before blaming the model?
options: Whether the right passage was retrieved at all
The sampling temperature used during generation
The parameter count of the underlying language model
Whether the prompt explicitly named the corpus being searched
quiz.explanation: If retrieval never surfaced the relevant passage, generation was never given a chance and no prompt engineering fixes it. Retrieval and generation must be scored separately — recall@k for retrieval, groundedness against retrieved text for generation.

quiz.question: The evidence base for ambient clinical documentation is strongest on which endpoint?
options: Accuracy of the clinical note against an independent reference
Clinician documentation burden and burnout
Accuracy of downstream billing and diagnostic coding
Diagnostic concordance between the scribe and the clinician
quiz.explanation: Burnout and documentation load are the well-supported endpoints, and they matter. Note accuracy and downstream consequences are much weaker — and there is a trap: a system can improve satisfaction while degrading record quality, since the clinicians best placed to notice are the ones relieved of checking.

quiz.question: In the AMIE study, what most limits the claim that an LLM outperformed physicians?
options: The sample of simulated consultations was too small to be conclusive
The specialist raters scoring the transcripts were not blinded
The physician comparator was also restricted to text chat
Only a single clinical specialty was represented in the scenarios
quiz.explanation: Patients were actors, the medium was text chat, and — decisively — physicians were confined to the same medium, without examination, gestalt or continuity. The honest statement is about synchronous text consultation, a real setting, not about being a better doctor.

quiz.question: What is the characteristic safety failure of patient-facing triage chatbots, and how must it be reported?
options: Over-triage, reported as specificity
Refusal to answer, reported as coverage
Latency, reported as time-to-advice
Under-triage, reported by acuity level
quiz.explanation: Under-triage of serious presentations is the recurring finding and the failure direction that matters. Triage is an ordered-outcome classification, so it owes a full confusion matrix by acuity — under- and over-triage carry entirely different costs and cannot be collapsed into accuracy.

quiz.question: Why should ROUGE or BLEU scores not reassure you about a generated clinical summary?
options: They measure overlap with a reference, not correctness
They are too computationally slow to run at scale
They require a human-written reference summary to exist
They systematically penalise appropriately brief summaries
quiz.explanation: A clinically dangerous omission barely moves an overlap score. The same caution applies to LLM-as-judge evaluation: convenient and increasingly standard, but it inherits the grader's blind spots. Both are evidence; neither is measurement.

lessons.title: Choosing an action — decision support, optimisation, and the off-policy trap
lessons.subtitle: The objective function is a policy document
lessons.description: Shape 6. Thresholds as value judgements, net benefit and the model that is worse than nothing, off-policy evaluation and why it invalidated the AI Clinician, and the honest evaluable half of the shape.
lessons.practical: Elicit pt for a decision you are involved in: how many unnecessary interventions would you accept per case found? Then check whether your current strategy beats treating everyone and treating nobody.

quiz.question: You would accept 9 unnecessary interventions to catch one true case. What is your threshold probability?
options: Nine per cent, matching the number of interventions accepted
Ten per cent, since pt equals one over N plus one
Ninety per cent, the complement of the acceptable error
It cannot be derived without knowing the outcome prevalence
quiz.explanation: pt = 1/(N+1) = 1/10. The threshold encodes the exchange rate between a missed case and an unnecessary intervention, so it is elicited from the relative harms rather than tuned — and it differs legitimately between a well-resourced hospital and a rural clinic.

quiz.question: Model A has better discrimination than Model B but negative net benefit above pt=0.20. What does negative net benefit mean?
options: Its calibration is poor and requires recalibration before use
Its confidence intervals include the null at that threshold
It performs worse than simply treating nobody at all
It requires a larger sample before the estimate stabilises
quiz.explanation: 'Treat nobody' scores exactly zero, always, and is the bar any model must clear. A negative net benefit means you would do less harm by switching the model off — and no summary of discrimination can reveal this, which is the point of the decision framing.

quiz.question: What is the off-policy evaluation problem?
options: Treatment policies change faster than models can be retrained
Policies cannot be represented in a supervised learning framework
Outcomes are censored, so long-run policy value is unidentifiable
Your data record the actions taken and nothing about those not taken
quiz.explanation: To evaluate a policy you need to know what happens when you follow it, but the data were generated by clinicians following their own policy. Where a learned policy diverges most from observed practice — exactly where its recommendations are interesting — there is almost no data, so the estimate is extrapolation dressed as measurement.

quiz.question: Which epidemiological bias is unavoidable when learning treatment policy from observational intensive-care data?
options: Confounding by indication, since treatment followed unmeasured severity
Recall bias, since the record is completed retrospectively
Differential loss to follow-up between treatment arms
Regression dilution from measurement error in the exposure
quiz.explanation: Clinicians chose treatments because of severity the model cannot see. It observes the treatment and the outcome but not the reason, and no algorithmic sophistication removes that — only randomisation, or a setting where the assignment mechanism is genuinely known.

quiz.question: Why is health close to the worst possible setting for reinforcement learning?
options: Health data are too high-dimensional for policy gradients to converge
Exploration means experimenting on patients, and the environment shifts
Reward functions in health cannot be expressed numerically at all
Electronic records lack the time resolution reinforcement learning needs
quiz.explanation: RL needs cheap exploration, many episodes, fast clear rewards and a stationary environment. Health offers experimentation on patients, one life per patient, delayed and contested outcomes, and continually changing practice, pathogens and policy. So health RL is almost always offline, which returns you to the off-policy problem.

quiz.question: What is the danger of optimising a stated objective exactly?
options: Solvers converge to local optima that are hard to detect
Optimisation requires constraints that are rarely known precisely
An incomplete objective is followed faithfully, abandoning what it omits
The optimum is unstable to small changes in input data
quiz.explanation: Maximise cases detected per euro and you will systematically abandon remote populations because they are expensive. That is not a bug in the solver — it is the objective being followed. Which is why writing the objective down explicitly is often the most valuable output of the exercise.

quiz.question: A paper reports an 'optimal' allocation strategy for screening resources. What should you look for first?
options: Whether the solver reached a certified global optimum
Whether the constraint set was validated against field data
Whether sensitivity analyses varied the input parameters
Whether the objective function is stated in the paper
quiz.explanation: An optimum is only defined relative to an objective, so an unstated objective makes 'optimal' meaningless — and it conceals a value judgement about whose outcomes count. The other three matter, but none of them can be interpreted until the objective is on the page.

lessons.title: Evaluation — the lesson that decides all the others
lessons.subtitle: Discrimination is a property of the model; everything that matters is a property of the model in a setting
lessons.description: Discrimination vs calibration, PPV at real prevalence, the validation ladder, leakage, dataset shift, proper scoring rules, net benefit, and TRIPOD+AI/PROBAST+AI.
lessons.practical: Take the most recent AI-in-health paper you read. Find its AUC, then its validation-set prevalence, whether calibration is reported, and whether validation was external. Time how long each takes to find.

quiz.question: A model's predicted probabilities are all multiplied by three. What happens to its AUC?
options: It is unchanged
It falls sharply
It rises
It becomes undefined
quiz.explanation: AUC is the Mann-Whitney U statistic and depends only on the ordering of predictions, never their values. Tripling every probability leaves ranks identical, so AUC is unchanged while calibration, PPV at a fixed threshold and alert burden are all destroyed.

quiz.question: Which quantity does a threshold-based decision actually require?
options: Discrimination
Calibration
The c-statistic
Sensitivity alone
quiz.explanation: Calibration tells you a predicted 0.7 corresponds to a 70% observed rate, which is what a decision rule needs. A perfectly discriminating but badly calibrated model tells you who is at higher risk without telling you whether anyone is at enough risk to act.

quiz.question: At 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity, PPV is 47.1% when prevalence is 10%. What is it at 0.1%?
options: About 8%
About 25%
About 0.8%
About 47% — PPV does not depend on prevalence
quiz.explanation: 0.79%. Sensitivity and specificity are unchanged; only the setting moved. Worse, the alert rate barely falls (17.0% to 10.1%) because it converges on the false-positive rate — the model keeps firing at similar volume while becoming almost entirely wrong.

quiz.question: What does internal cross-validation estimate?
options: Performance on data like the development data
Whether the model changes outcomes
Calibration under dataset shift
Performance in a new health system
quiz.explanation: It corrects optimism, not generalisability. The Epic Sepsis Model reached this rung and was marketed as though impact-evaluated; external validation across a large health system found much weaker discrimination, poor calibration and a heavy alert burden.

quiz.question: A sepsis prediction model uses antibiotic orders as a predictor. What is the defect?
options: Leakage — the order followed the suspicion
Collinearity between the antibiotic and severity predictors
Immortal time bias introduced by the observation window
Non-linearity in the relationship between dose and outcome
quiz.explanation: The order exists because someone already suspected sepsis, so the model receives information about the outcome it could never have in true prospective use. Leakage produces spectacular, entirely fake performance and is hard to see from a methods section.

quiz.question: Why does evaluating a point forecast with MAE reward over-confidence?
options: MAE is unduly sensitive to a small number of outliers
There is no penalty for a too-narrow interval
MAE ignores the mean of the predictive distribution entirely
MAE cannot be computed for count-valued forecast targets
quiz.explanation: A forecast is a distribution and must be scored as one. Proper rules — log score, CRPS, WIS for quantiles — cannot be gamed, because the best expected score comes from reporting your honest belief. Coverage of the 50% and 95% intervals should also be checked.

quiz.question: A dermatology model reports 94% overall accuracy. What is the most important missing number?
options: The number of images in the training set
The learning-rate schedule used during training
Performance by Fitzpatrick skin type
The number of diagnostic classes the model distinguishes
quiz.explanation: Aggregate accuracy is a weighted average that hides who the model fails. Training sets skew to lighter skin, and the deeper problem is that performance on darker skin is frequently not measured at all — so the failure is invisible rather than merely known.

quiz.question: A vendor claims 92% accuracy for an outcome occurring in 3% of patients. What is the sharpest reply?
options: Ask for the AUC on the same validation cohort instead
Ask for a substantially larger external validation set
Ask whether the model was regularised during development
Note that predicting 'no' for everyone scores 97%
quiz.explanation: The trivial constant classifier beats the product, which shows accuracy is the wrong metric on imbalanced outcomes. Asking for AUC is an improvement but still insufficient — you need calibration and PPV at the deployment prevalence.

quiz.question: What is meant by 'six shapes, six debts'?
options: Each shape owes a specific kind of evaluation
Each shape requires exactly six evaluation metrics
There are six distinct reporting frameworks to apply
Each of the six shapes requires six lessons to cover
quiz.explanation: Once you know a claim's shape, you know what evaluation it owes. Shape 1 owes a false-alarm rate and timeliness at a matched threshold; shape 2 a proper scoring rule and a naive baseline; shape 3 calibration and PPV at deployment prevalence; shape 4 replication; shape 5 a definition of correct; shape 6 an account of evaluation without deployment.

lessons.title: Deployment, bias and governance — what happens when it is wrong, and who finds out
lessons.subtitle: Nearly every failure in this course is a failure of the surrounding system
lessons.description: The AI chasm, four kinds of bias with four different fixes, human factors, the EU regulatory tiers and the naming problem, and the seven conditions that got TB CAD to a WHO recommendation.
lessons.practical: Take any Atlas entry and answer the governing question in two sentences: what happens when it is wrong, and who finds out?

quiz.question: Where does the AI chasm sit on the validation ladder?
options: Between apparent performance and internal cross-validation
Between external validation and impact evaluation
Between temporal validation and geographical validation
Between regulatory clearance and commercial procurement
quiz.explanation: Almost the entire published literature sits below impact evaluation. A paper needs a dataset and a metric; a deployment needs an integration, a threshold, a workflow, a trained user, monitoring, escalation and a maintenance budget. When someone says 'clinically validated', ask which rung they mean.

quiz.question: Which kind of bias has a genuinely clean technical fix, and what is it?
options: Representation bias — reweight the training distribution
Deployment bias — retrain on data from the target site
Label bias — change the target variable
Feedback loops — add a regularisation penalty
quiz.explanation: Obermeyer's disparity largely disappeared on relabelling to a health-based target. The others need data collection, fieldwork or institutional will: representation bias needs measurement then collection, deployment bias needs workflow study, and feedback loops need deliberate exploration against the model's own advice.

quiz.question: How does the feedback loop appear in surveillance specifically?
options: Reporting delay causes recent counts to appear artificially low
Case definitions tighten as programmes approach elimination targets
Laboratory capacity declines faster than case counts fall
Screening goes where cases were reported, generating more reports there
quiz.explanation: The model sends teams to previously positive areas, which produces more detections there, which confirms the model, while unsurveyed areas stay quiet and therefore stay unsurveyed. The fix is to allocate some effort against the model's advice — which means knowingly spending sub-optimally by its own criterion.

quiz.question: When is automation bias strongest?
options: When the model's output is plausible and the user is tired or junior
When the model's confidence scores are poorly calibrated
When the interface presents several competing recommendations
When the user has been trained on the model's known limitations
quiz.explanation: People defer to a confident machine against their own correct judgement, and defer more when busy, tired or junior — exactly when the model is meant to help. The effect is strongest for plausible wrong answers, which is precisely what modern systems produce.

quiz.question: Ambient scribes are widely deployed while AMIE, with a randomised trial, is not. Why?
options: Scribes were shown to improve patient outcomes in trials
The regulatory class follows the claim, not what the thing can break
Diagnostic models consistently fail external validation
Health systems will not fund diagnostic decision support
quiz.explanation: Writing a note is 'documentation' and generally not a regulated device; producing a differential is 'diagnosis' and lands in the EU AI Act's high-risk tier. The consequence is inverted — the product with less oversight is the one in the room with patients — so the reviewer's question is whether the classification matches the risk.

quiz.question: What is absent from the seven conditions that got TB CAD to a WHO recommendation?
options: Any requirement for multi-site external validation
Any requirement for subgroup performance reporting
Any claim about the model architecture
Any requirement for a locally tunable threshold
quiz.explanation: All seven concern the label's independence, acquisition, population match, threshold tunability, a confirmatory step downstream, subgroup reporting and a guideline home. None is about the network. Which is the course's argument in one observation.

quiz.question: When does a human-in-the-loop control become decorative?
options: When the reviewer lacks training in the model's failure modes
When the review step is not logged for later audit
When the model's output exceeds a certain volume per shift
When the product's value proposition is not having to review
quiz.explanation: If the safety case is 'the clinician reviews the output' while the reason for buying the product is to stop doing that work, the control cannot function. Ambient documentation is the live example: review is both the safety mechanism and the thing being sold away.

lessons.title: Deep dive — Google Flu Trends
lessons.subtitle: The parable: what a proxy can and cannot replace
lessons.description: Full arc from research question to conclusion. Why it under-estimated 2009 and doubled the 2012-13 peak, and what the approach is actually worth.
lessons.practical: Explain the case out loud in 60 seconds using section 10, without notes. If you cannot say why it failed in BOTH directions, re-read sections 6 and 7.

quiz.question: Google Flu Trends failed twice, in opposite directions. What were the two failures?
options: It failed only in 2012-13; the 2009 performance was accurate but arrived too late
It over-estimated 2009 and under-estimated 2012-13, both from search-volume drift
It over-estimated both seasons, increasingly, as the model aged without recalibration
It under-estimated the 2009 pandemic and over-estimated the 2012-13 peak
quiz.explanation: It under-estimated the 2009 swine flu pandemic because the event was out of season and the model had only ever learned normal winters — so the one event it existed to catch was the one it could not catch. Then in 2012-13 it over-estimated the peak by roughly double.

quiz.question: Why does the deep dive describe the 2009 under-estimate as structural rather than bad luck?
options: Pandemic influenza produces a different symptom profile, so the population searched an entirely different set of terms
It was fitted on seasonal influenza, so an out-of-season pandemic was outside everything it had learned
The model was retrained annually and 2009 fell between two retraining cycles
The search index had not yet accumulated enough historical volume to fit on
quiz.explanation: The model learned the relationship between search volume and ILI across normal winters. A pandemic arriving out of season is precisely the case with no analogue in the training data — which is why the failure is a property of the design rather than of that particular year.

quiz.question: Two causes are given for the 2012-13 over-estimate. What are they?
options: Overfitting to the 2009 pandemic, and a shift in the age distribution of searchers
Predictors selected for correlation rather than sense, and Google changing what searchers saw
A change in the CDC's ILI case definition, and reduced clinic attendance that season
Loss of the original engineering team, and migration to a new data warehouse
quiz.explanation: Predictors chosen by correlation alone have no reason to keep working when the world shifts. And Google kept changing what people saw when they searched — autocomplete, suggested terms, related searches — so the inputs quietly changed meaning underneath a model nobody was recalibrating.

quiz.question: What does the deep dive say the lesson is NOT?
options: That 'big data does not work'
That unstable predictors are a hazard when selected purely by correlation
That proxies require the real measurement to stay honest
That a nowcast can supplement surveillance but not replace it
quiz.explanation: The failure was not about volume of data. It was about a proxy drifting away from what it proxied, with no ground truth left in place to notice. That is why the durable conclusion is that a proxy can supplement surveillance and can never replace it.

quiz.question: Google Flu Trends is described in the course as the canonical shape-straddling failure. What does that mean here?
options: It combined tabular and text data in one model without ever declaring which of the two dominated the prediction
It was evaluated on whether it tracked ILI, and marketed on whether it warned earlier
It reported accuracy on one population and calibration on another
It switched from a regression to a classification framing partway through
quiz.explanation: Tracking ILI is shape 2, forecasting. Warning earlier than surveillance is shape 1, detecting the unusual. Those require different evidence, and a claim evaluated as one shape and sold as another is the most common failure mode in the field.

quiz.question: What is the appropriate present-day reading of this case for a surveillance programme?
options: The approach works if the model is retrained continuously on recent data
Digital proxies are unusable for public health and should not be resourced
Digital proxies are usable where a ground truth is maintained alongside them
The failure was specific to search data; social media proxies avoid it
quiz.explanation: Retraining helps but does not solve it, because retraining needs the ground truth the proxy was meant to replace. The honest position is that a proxy earns its place as a supplement to a maintained measurement, and loses it the moment the measurement is switched off.

lessons.title: Deep dive — Two imaging stories: chest X-ray and skin
lessons.subtitle: Both matched specialists. Only one reached practice. The difference is not accuracy
lessons.description: TB CAD reached WHO recommendation and scale; dermatology AI mostly did not. Seven structural conditions explain why, and none of them is model performance.
lessons.practical: Take any AI application you have read about and score it against the seven conditions in section 8. The count predicts whether it will reach practice better than its AUC does.

quiz.question: Chest X-ray AI for TB reached scale and dermatology AI largely did not, despite both matching specialists. What does the deep dive identify as the decisive difference?
options: The volume of training data available in each speciality
The regulatory route each product chose to pursue, and how long clearance took in each case
The pathway each was placed in, not the accuracy either achieved
The absolute accuracy achieved on external validation sets
quiz.explanation: Both matched specialists on accuracy. The TB system was built as a triage step with a confirmatory laboratory test behind it; the skin apps were built to be the answer itself. Whether medical AI helps anyone depends far more on the pathway you put it in than on how good the model is.

quiz.question: What is the practical consequence of the TB system being a triage step rather than a diagnosis?
options: It removes the need for country-specific threshold setting, since a single global cut-off can then be applied
When it is wrong it costs a molecular test, rather than a missed cancer
It can be deployed without regulatory clearance in most jurisdictions
It requires a lower accuracy threshold, so evaluation is less demanding
quiz.explanation: It gives a score, each country sets its own cut-off, and anyone flagged gets a molecular test. The cost of a false positive is a test. For a skin app built as the answer itself, at a fixed threshold with no laboratory behind it, the cost of a false negative is someone with a melanoma being told not to worry.

quiz.question: The two applications also differed in what they were validated against. How?
options: Both against expert consensus, but TB used more experts per image
TB against prospective outcomes; dermatology against retrospective chart review
TB against a laboratory result; dermatology largely against clinicians' opinions
TB against dermatologist consensus; dermatology against biopsy results
quiz.explanation: TB models were validated against a culture or molecular result — an objective reference. Dermatology models were largely validated against dermatologists' opinions, which is a comparator that inherits the comparator's own error and cannot exceed it.

quiz.question: What does the deep dive say about the populations each was trained on?
options: TB models were trained on the populations they would be used in; dermatology mostly on light skin
Dermatology models were trained on more diverse populations but tested on fewer
TB models used synthetic augmentation; dermatology used only real images
Both were trained on image sets assembled to be globally representative of the populations they would serve
quiz.explanation: And the compounding detail is that skin type was often not even recorded, so the gap could not be seen in the evaluation. A subgroup failure you have no field for is a subgroup failure nobody will find.

quiz.question: Which finding best illustrates that a dermatology model can learn the wrong thing entirely?
options: Accuracy fell sharply whenever images were resized below the resolution the model had been trained at
Surgical skin markings raised melanoma probability and increased false positives on benign lesions
Performance varied by anatomical site more than by lesion type
Models performed worse on images captured with older camera hardware
quiz.explanation: Clinicians mark lesions they are already concerned about, so the marking is a proxy for clinical suspicion rather than for melanoma. The model learned the marking. It is the cleanest demonstration in the course that high accuracy can rest on a feature that will not be there — or will be there for the wrong reason — in deployment.

quiz.question: What should a programme take from this pair when assessing any new diagnostic AI?
options: Require external validation on at least three independent datasets from different health systems
Ask what happens when it is wrong, and what sits downstream to catch it
Prefer applications where the model matches or exceeds specialist accuracy
Choose applications with an existing regulatory clearance in a comparable market
quiz.explanation: External validation and accuracy both matter, but they are not what separated these two cases. The separating question is about the pathway: what the failure costs, and whether anything downstream catches it. That is the question the whole course is organised around.

lessons.title: Deep dive — The consultation: AMIE and the ambient scribe
lessons.subtitle: One proved without shipping. The other shipped without proving. The difference is what you call it
lessons.description: AMIE has a randomised blinded trial and no deployment; ambient scribes have enormous deployment and thin evidence on note accuracy. The regulatory class is set by the claim, not the risk — so the less-overseen product is the one in the room with patients.
lessons.practical: Take the 60-second explanation in section 10 and deliver it out loud to a colleague. The test of understanding is whether they grasp the naming argument without you re-reading section 7.

quiz.question: AMIE has a randomised blinded trial and no deployment; ambient scribes have enormous deployment and thin accuracy evidence. What best explains the inversion?
options: The regulatory class is set by the product's claim, not by what it can break
Ambient scribes use a fundamentally simpler and safer technology
Diagnostic models have consistently failed external validation
Health systems will not pay for diagnostic support of any kind
quiz.explanation: Writing a note is 'documentation', so a scribe is generally not a regulated medical device and needs no clinical validation. Producing a differential is 'diagnosis', which triggers the high-risk tier under the EU AI Act and MDR, or the FDA SaMD route. The consequence is inverted: the product with less oversight is the one touching patients.

quiz.question: In an ambient scribe pipeline, which error is hardest to detect and why?
options: Fabricated findings, because they are clinically implausible
Omission, because a note missing the key sentence looks entirely normal
Speaker mis-attribution, because it is rare in practice
Transcription errors, because they are corrected downstream
quiz.explanation: The summarisation step's job is to discard the large majority of what was said, so leaving out the one sentence that mattered produces a note with nothing anomalous about it. Fabrication is detectable; omission is invisible — and omission rates are almost never reported.

quiz.question: Why is 'the clinician reviews and signs the note' a weak safety control here?
options: Clinicians lack the training to spot summarisation errors
Signing is a legal formality with no clinical content
The product's value proposition is precisely not having to read and type
The review happens too long after the encounter to be useful
quiz.explanation: The safety case rests on a review performed by someone who adopted the product to stop doing that work. When the human-in-the-loop step is the thing being sold away, the control becomes decorative — and automation bias makes confident output likelier to be signed unread.

quiz.question: AMIE matched or exceeded physicians on several empathy and communication measures. What is the least mystical explanation?
options: Language models are optimised directly for empathic phrasing during training
Patient actors systematically prefer written to spoken clinical communication
Empathy ratings are too unreliable to support any comparison at all
It has unlimited patience, no time pressure, and no previous patient
quiz.explanation: Never tired, never rushed, no prior difficult consultation and no hunger are structural advantages in a rated conversation. That does not make the finding invalid — it makes it interpretable, and it suggests the comparison is partly about working conditions rather than about capability.

quiz.question: What did the AMIE trial's text-chat design do to the strength of its conclusion?
options: It made the comparison fairer and simultaneously narrowed what it can support
It invalidated the comparison, since physicians never work this way
It had no material effect, because history-taking is purely verbal anyway
It biased results toward the physicians, who are trained writers
quiz.explanation: Confining both arms to text removes a medium advantage, which is methodologically defensible. It also bounds the conclusion tightly to synchronous text consultation with simulated patients — a real and growing setting, but not general clinical practice. Both statements are true and both should be said.

quiz.question: Where is ambient documentation's value best quantified?
options: Words per note reduced compared with typed notes
Clinician-hours returned, especially after-hours work
Reduction in diagnostic error rate across encounters
Improvement in patient satisfaction with the consultation
quiz.explanation: The units of the decision are clinician-hours. One to two minutes across twenty encounters a day is 20-40 minutes daily, and the after-hours reduction matters most because that is where attrition is generated. In a system short of clinicians that is a workforce intervention, not a gadget.

quiz.question: What is the specifically epidemiological harm if scribes are used unevenly across populations?
options: Reduced statistical power in studies using those records
Loss of patient consent for secondary use of the data
Differential misclassification entering every dataset built from those records
Increased missingness that standard imputation cannot handle
quiz.explanation: If omission rates are worse for accented speech, interpreted consultations or interrupted encounters, the error is non-random with respect to population. Every study built on those records inherits it as differential misclassification — a bias arriving through the back door, in the records rather than the analysis.

quiz.question: AMIE's training used self-play: a model as doctor, a model as patient, a model as critic. What is the central hazard?
options: Simulated consultations are far too short to resemble real clinical encounters
Patient personas cannot be varied enough for the training to generalise
Self-play cannot be scaled to cover a broad enough range of conditions
A shared blind spot can be amplified rather than corrected
quiz.explanation: Being graded by a model on scenarios written by a model can reinforce a common error rather than expose it. This is precisely why the external randomised evaluation against real physicians carries all the evidential weight — and why running one was to the authors' credit.

lessons.title: Deep dive — Two database failures: Epic Sepsis and Obermeyer
lessons.subtitle: One was never checked. The other was checked, and answered the wrong question
lessons.description: The two distinct ways a tabular health model goes wrong. A governance failure and a construct-validity failure, and why a rule that catches one misses the other.
topics: Fixing the label not the model
lessons.practical: Take a risk score used where you work. Write down (a) what its target variable literally is, and (b) what you actually care about. If they differ, name the wedge between them.

quiz.question: Epic's sepsis model had no biological reference standard, so sepsis was defined from clinician actions. What does the model therefore predict?
options: Clinician recognition of sepsis, which is what you did not need a model for
Sepsis onset several hours before it becomes clinically apparent to the team
Mortality risk that is independent of the treating team's own behaviour
Antibiotic resistance patterns prevailing in the admitting clinical unit
quiz.explanation: If the label is derived from the behaviour you want to improve, the model can only learn to imitate that behaviour. It cannot beat clinicians at recognising sepsis when the definition of sepsis is that clinicians recognised it.

quiz.question: At the deployed threshold the model alerted on ~18% of admissions with ~33% sensitivity, sepsis occurring in ~7%. Roughly how many alerts per true case?
options: About two
About eight
About twenty
About fifty
quiz.explanation: Derived: 180 alerts per 1,000 admissions, of which about 23 are real sepsis — roughly 8 alerts per true case, an implied PPV near 13%, with about 47 sepsis cases missed entirely. AUC reports none of this, and alert fatigue makes it worse than neutral.

quiz.question: Obermeyer's algorithm was accurate at predicting its target. Why was that not a defence?
options: Its accuracy was only ever measured internally and never on external data
No calibration analysis was reported anywhere in the original publication
Its target was healthcare cost, used as a proxy for health need
The training data were too old to reflect contemporary clinical practice
quiz.explanation: The model was never broken; it answered the question it was given, and the question encoded the inequity. At equal illness less is spent on Black patients because of unequal access, so cost is a biased measure of need — and the bias has a direction.

quiz.question: What single change removed most of the disparity in the Obermeyer case?
options: Adding race as an explicit predictor to correct for it
Rebalancing the training set across racial groups
Applying a different decision threshold per group
Retraining on a health-based rather than cost-based target
quiz.explanation: Relabelling. Predicting a direct health measure instead of cost removed roughly 84% of the disparity, and auto-enrolment of Black patients went from 17.7% to 46.5% — a 2.6-fold change driven by the target, not the model.

quiz.question: The Obermeyer team did not have the model's weights. How did they audit it?
options: They compared its scores against independent health measures it was never trained on
They reverse-engineered the feature importances from the predictions
They obtained the source code under a research agreement
They rebuilt an equivalent model from public claims data
quiz.explanation: They took the predictions and asked whether patients at the same score were equally sick, using chronic-condition counts and biomarkers as an independent yardstick. That is the transferable technique: you do not need the weights, you need the predictions and a construct the model was not trained on.

quiz.question: Why will a rule requiring external validation before deployment not have prevented the Obermeyer failure?
options: Because the algorithm was not classified as a medical device
Because external validation would have confirmed it predicted cost well
Because claims data cannot be validated across sites
Because the disparity only emerged after several years of use
quiz.explanation: It was a construct-validity failure, not a validation failure. The model transferred fine; the target was wrong. Epic needed external validation; Obermeyer needed someone to interrogate the target variable. A governance rule that catches one does not catch the other.

quiz.question: Which generalisation of the Obermeyer mechanism bears most directly on surveillance epidemiology?
options: Cost data are simply unavailable in most low- and middle-income systems
Claims-based models cannot be transferred to infectious disease settings
Any proxy target inherits the inequities of the process that generated it
Risk scores need recalibrating whenever local coding practice changes
quiz.explanation: Cost proxies need; diagnosis proxies disease, but only where people can reach a diagnosis; reported cases proxy incidence, but only where surveillance reaches. The last is the working epidemiologist's version of exactly this failure.

lessons.title: Deep dive — Two that worked: forecast hubs and wastewater
lessons.subtitle: One won by changing the institution, the other by changing the sample. Neither by changing the model
lessons.description: The positive cases. Why prospective public scoring fixed a field, and why testing sewage beat a decade of algorithmic early warning — with both sets of limits stated as specifically as the findings.
topics: Lead time that can be acted on
